I'm in Santiago, Chile at 2026-04-05 06:09 -04 (UTC-0400) (2026-04-05T10:09:00Z in UTC), at latitude -33.4489 degrees and longitude -70.6693 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is -10.39 degrees and its azimuth is 89.833 degrees, so it is below the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 48.296 degrees and its azimuth is 271.847 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 89.48 percent illuminated, 142.04 degrees from the Sun, and 398237.5 kilometers away. The sky brightness is nautical twilight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Based on the data you provided, **yes, you should have a very good chance of spotting the Moon!**

Here is the breakdown of why you should be able to see it:

### 1. The Altitude (Height in the sky)
An altitude of **48.3 degrees** is quite high. For context, if you imagine the horizon as 0° and directly overhead as 90°, the Moon is almost exactly halfway up the sky. It won't be hugging the horizon (where atmospheric haze can make it harder to see); it will be prominent in the sky.

### 2. The Azimuth (Direction)
An azimuth of **271.8 degrees** means the Moon is positioned almost directly to your **West** (which is 270°). Since you are in Santiago and the Sun is currently below the horizon to the East, the Moon is positioned in the opposite direction, making it the dominant feature of the western sky.

### 3. The Phase and Illumination
At **89.48% illumination**, the Moon is in its "Waxing Gibbous" phase, very close to being a Full Moon. This means it will be extremely bright and easy to distinguish from the background stars.

### 4. Sky Conditions (Nautical Twilight)
You mentioned the sky is in **nautical twilight**. This is the period when the sun is between 6 and 12 degrees below the horizon. During nautical twilight, the sky is dark enough that the Moon will appear very bright, but there is still a slight "glow" in the atmosphere. Because the Moon is nearly full and high in the sky, it will stand out sharply against the darkening blue/grey of the twilight.

### Summary for your viewing:
Look toward the **West**. Because it is nearly full and at a high altitude, it should be the most striking object in the sky. Even with "normal unaided eyesight," a Moon that is 89% illuminated at a 48-degree altitude is impossible to miss!

**Enjoy the view!**
